query: For initially solid iron–nickel–chromium–cobalt–copper high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles examined across the premelting and melting regime, limited understanding of their thermal response constrains interpretation of application limits and high-temperature synthesis, where cooling must consolidate the solid solution. Prior studies of Ag, Au, Al, and Pd nanoparticles established that nanoscale phase-transition behavior can differ markedly among particle systems, but findings from single-metal particles do not resolve the response of chemically complex nanoparticles. Work on bimetallic particles further demonstrated that chemical complexity can produce varied configurations, while research on high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles remains sparse and has not established the governing physics for this composition. What single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs its premelting and melting behavior and why? Define a controlled comparison, predicted observations relative to a baseline particle, the limits within which the hypothesis should apply, prior findings that support it, and an observation that would decisively falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: In equiatomic Fe–Ni–Cr–Co–Cu high-entropy-alloy (HEA) nanoparticles, premelting and the subsequent complete melting are governed by kinetic surface segregation of the lowest-melting, lowest-surface-energy element (Cu). Cu enrichment at the outer ~1 nm lowers the local cohesive energy, triggering a surface-confined, liquid-like layer (premelting) at temperatures well below the bulk solidus, while the configurational-entropy-stabilised, Cu-depleted core melts only at higher temperature. Thus the overall thermal response is a two-step process controlled by Cu surface concentration.
generation.material_initial_state: Chemically homogeneous, 10 ± 2 nm diameter, equiatomic Fe₀.₂Ni₀.₂Cr₀.₂Co₀.₂Cu₀.₂ solid-solution nanoparticles produced by rapid inert-gas condensation; crystal structure: fcc; no oxide shell.
generation.intervention: Controlled in-situ heating of individual unsupported nanoparticles in a transmission electron microscope (TEM) from 300 K to 1700 K at 5 K min⁻¹.
generation.conditions: High vacuum (<10⁻⁶ mbar) to suppress oxidation; beam dosage kept below 5 e⁻ Å⁻² s⁻¹ to minimise radiolysis; particle size distribution within ±20 %.
generation.structural_mediator: Time- and temperature-dependent Cu surface enrichment layer (~1 nm thick) quantified by spatially-resolved EDX/EELS.
generation.mechanism: 1. On heating, surface diffusion is faster than bulk diffusion, allowing Cu atoms (lowest γ and Tₘ) to segregate to the surface to minimise Gibbs free energy. 2. The Cu-rich shell has reduced cohesive energy and lower local Tₘ, so it transforms into a quasi-liquid layer (premelting). 3. Latent-heat absorption and the liquid shell accelerate further Cu diffusion, but the high configurational entropy of the core resists chemical partitioning, delaying core melting until higher T. 4. Complete melting occurs when the advancing solid–liquid interface reaches the core once sufficient Cu has accumulated at the interface or the core itself reaches its reduced size-dependent melting temperature.
generation.predicted_outcome: TEM imaging will show the onset of surface faceting loss and increased mean-square atomic displacement (via nanodiffraction or Debye-Waller analysis) at T₁ ≈ 0.8 T_bulk(FeNiCrCoCu) for Cu-containing HEA NPs, followed by full particle liquefaction at T₂ ≈ 0.9 T_bulk. A control HEA nanoparticle with the same elements but Cu replaced by equal parts Fe, Ni, Cr, and Co will exhibit a single melting event at T* ≈ T₂ (no early premelting). Surface EDX/EELS will reveal ≥50 at.% Cu enrichment at T₁ in the Cu-containing particles but no comparable enrichment in the Cu-free control.
generation.baseline: Cu-free Fe–Ni–Cr–Co HEA nanoparticles of the same size heated identically.
generation.boundary: Particle diameters 5–30 nm; heating rates ≤50 K min⁻¹; vacuum or inert atmosphere; compositions in which Cu is the sole element with Tₘ < 1550 K and γ < 2 J m⁻².
generation.uncertainty: Magnitude of the temperature offset (T₂–T₁) is estimated (≈150–250 K) from analogous Ag surface-premelting literature; actual value may vary with particle size and residual oxides. Competing segregation of Ni (also moderate γ) could partially moderate the effect.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two batches of 10 nm HEA nanoparticles: (a) equiatomic FeNiCrCoCu, (b) equiatomic FeNiCrCo (no Cu). Heat each batch in identical in-situ TEM experiments. Concurrently acquire (i) bright-field videos, (ii) nanobeam diffraction patterns every 25 K, (iii) spectrum-imaging EDX maps after each 50 K step.
measurements: Onset temperature of diffuse diffraction halo (premelting) for each particle
Surface (outer 1 nm) Cu atomic fraction vs temperature
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: The hypothesis is falsified if either: (1) The Cu-containing particles do NOT exhibit an earlier, surface-confined premelting transition (no distinct T₁ before T₂) OR (2) Measured Cu surface enrichment remains ≤10 at.% at all temperatures prior to full melting. Observing either outcome would refute the proposed Cu-segregation-controlled mechanism.
